item.title: We desperately need water : Nacula resident calls for urgent Government assistance
item.description: Josateki Vakatauvata says he lived in Lautoka for most of his life before returning to Nacula in 2019 to look after his mother, and has since experienced first-hand how difficult the dry season can be for island communities. Vakatauvata says this has been one of the hardest dry periods for the area, with some water sources drying up.
item.content:encoded:
Josateki Vakatauvata says he lived in Lautoka for most of his life before returning to Nacula in 2019 to look after his mother, and has since experienced first-hand how difficult the dry season can be for island communities.

Vakatauvata says this has been one of the hardest dry periods for the area, with some water sources drying up.

He says officials from the Water Authority of Fiji visited the area yesterday to assess water sources, including those used by schools.

Vakatauvata says Yasawa North Secondary School and Ratu Meli Memorial Primary School each have more than 100 students, including more than 20 boarders at each school.

He says despite the water shortage, students continue to attend classes while the schools try to manage with the limited water available.

Vakatauvata says Nacula Village still has access to a water source, but the situation is more serious around Government facilities in the area.

He says the health centre, staff quarters and police post have run out of water after a small borehole they relied on dried up.

Vakatauvata says despite the difficult conditions, the nurses have continued providing services at the health centre as people in Yasawa may still need medical assistance.

He says bottled drinking water has been provided for patients and health staff, but staff still need water for cooking, washing and cleaning.

Vakatauvata says some rain over the past few days has provided temporary relief, but it has not been enough to resolve the shortage.

Insert: (VitiFM) Vakatauvata on assistance)

He is calling on the Government to urgently provide clean water and additional water tanks to affected communities.

This comes after Government assessments found more than 4,900 people across 23 villages in Yasawa were affected by water shortages caused by the prolonged dry weather.

Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Management Mosese Bulitavu had earlier said Nacula, Naviti, Yasawa and Viwa were among the most affected areas, with eight nursing stations, 10 primary schools, two secondary schools and two infant schools also affected.

Bulitavu had said the Ministry was working with the Government Shipping Service to secure a vessel to transport water to affected communities, while private barges and other suitable vessels were also being considered.

Water assistance has since been delivered to Batiki, while fijivillage News is seeking an update on when further assistance will reach affected communities in Yasawa and Taveuni.

fijivillage News has sent follow-up questions to the Ministry of Rural ans Maritime Development and Disaster Management, seeking an update on the planned water assistance for Yasawa and Taveuni.

item.title: Turaga confirms changes to court exhibit security after missing cocaine
item.description: Following the incident involving the missing cocaine from an exhibit at the Suva High Court, changes are being implemented and Police are taking proactive steps. Minister for Justice Siromi Turaga has confirmed this while responding to questions in Parliament on what immediate steps has the Ministry taken to review and upgrade security protocols within the judiciary, including evidence storage and
item.content:encoded:
Following the incident involving the missing cocaine from an exhibit at the Suva High Court, changes are being implemented and Police are taking proactive steps.

Minister for Justice Siromi Turaga has confirmed this while responding to questions in Parliament on what immediate steps has the Ministry taken to review and upgrade security protocols within the judiciary, including evidence storage and chain-of-custody procedures.

While highlighting other incidents, Turaga says this issue is not new and is showing the magnitude of the problem.

When questioned by Opposition MP Faiyaz Koya if a complete and thorough assessment will be conducted on all evidence in the exhibit, Turaga says following the incident, he called a meeting with the Chief Registrar, Acting Director of Public Prosecutions, Commissioner of Police and Permanent Secretary for Justice and further meetings followed, and changes are now being put in place.

He says Police have taken steps to control exhibits in designated areas, rather than keeping them at individual stations as they did previously.

The Minister also says the judiciary has begun reviewing its protocols for storing, handling, moving and releasing exhibits and other evidence and the Chief Registrar has assessed arrangements across the relevant registries, including storage, records, chain of custody, CCTV coverage and physical security.

He says the assessment aims to identify gaps and determine what additional safeguards are needed.

The Minister says a report is being prepared to set out the required improvements.

Turaga says work to improve security at the criminal registry began yesterday, and is progressing.

The Minister says there were initial delays in procuring and approving IT-related security equipment and systems, but these matters have now progressed.

He says the review is also considering staff responsibilities, incident reporting and regular monitoring.

Turaga says the judiciary will address identified gaps through appropriate administrative measures, including stronger procedures and staff awareness and will continue to document and review concerns and, where necessary, refer them for investigation by the appropriate authorities, while respecting due process and judicial independence.

He has also expressed his disappointment and shock at the missing $31 million worth of cocaine from the Suva Court House.

He says the Prime Minister was informed this morning, and police investigations are ongoing.

Turaga is asking members to allow that investigation to proceed and promises that no stone will be left unturned, and anyone found responsible will be held accountable.

item.title: Counter-Narcotics Bill debate on Thursday, Opposition calls for delay until Nov
item.description: The Counter-Narcotics Bill, which establishes the Counter-Narcotics Bureau, has been tabled in Parliament under Parliamentary Standing Order 51 and will be debated on Thursday. While tabling the Bill, Minister for Policing Ioane Naivalurua says the Bureau will be a dedicated institution that will serve as Fiji's special agency for coordinating national efforts, developing specialised intelligence
item.content:encoded:
The Counter-Narcotics Bill, which establishes the Counter-Narcotics Bureau, has been tabled in Parliament under Parliamentary Standing Order 51 and will be debated on Thursday.

While tabling the Bill, Minister for Policing Ioane Naivalurua says the Bureau will be a dedicated institution that will serve as Fiji's special agency for coordinating national efforts, developing specialised intelligence and investigative capabilities, strengthening partnership across government and internationally, and advancing a comprehensive response to the growing narcotics threat.

He says without the enactment of the Bill, the Government will face continuing limitations on the operationalisation of the Bureau as a legally established and properly mandated institution.

Naivalurua says the longer the legislative response is delayed, the longer Fiji remains dependent on an outdated legal framework while the threat continues to evolve.

He says the Bill is being tabled under Order 51 is to ensure that the legislative response is not unnecessarily delayed, adding the illicit drug challenge is no longer solely a law enforcement matter but is a national crisis and a national security concern.

While opposing the tabling of the Bill under Standing Order 51, Opposition MP Jone Usamate says bringing a Bill of this magnitude to Parliament and asking MPs to debate it within two days suggests that Parliament is not needed to properly consider Bills.

He says if the Government had done its job well, they could be debating it at least at the next meeting in November, giving the representatives of the people in Parliament the opportunity to scrutinize it in a much better fashion.

Opposition MP Alvick Maharaj also says under Order 51, it can also be fast-tracked through a committee within 30 days and brought back to the Parliament.

He says they have almost eight Bills to debate on Thursday, for which they have to prepare themselves.

Maharaj says the 200-page Bill should be referred to a committee for 30 days to allow proper scrutiny before being brought back to Parliament in November.

Opposition MP Premila Kumar says she thought she was intelligent, but today she gives up, asking how they are going to read this Bill, as well as the other Bills, considering they are in Parliament every day, go home very late, are tired, and then have to read the Bills.

She says, as representatives of the people, they have to do that, even if it means getting only two or three hours of sleep.

Kumar says the Bill should have gone through public consultation to raise awareness and allow people to understand its different provisions, adding that this opportunity has been missed.

Acting Attorney General Siromi Turaga says it is unfair to criticise the legal drafters for the time taken to prepare the Bill, saying they are passionate about their work and have other responsibilities.

He says the Government has been given an opportunity to consider and comment on the Bill, adding that most of its provisions are not entirely new and are already part of existing laws.

Turaga says the Government needs to make a decision and move forward, adding that the Bill is needed for the new department to begin making key decisions.

Opposition MP Ketan Lal says people must be consulted on this Bill, also adding that the Opposition does not have the resources in their Parliamentary Office to analyse this Bill within 48 hours.

Leader of Opposition Inia Seruiratu says the Bill refers to the Accountability and Transparency Commission, as well as the Code of Conduct, under Section 23.

He says he asked about the Code of Conduct earlier today, noting that it has been sitting in the Solicitor-General’s Office for months, despite being referred to in the Bill.

Seruiratu says the Accountability and Transparency Commission, provided for under Section 121 of the Constitution, has also not been activated.

He says these are among the reasons why Parliament should allow one month for a committee to scrutinise the Bill.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Tourism Viliame Gavoka says Fiji’s declaration of an emergency over HIV and drugs received global coverage, including on CNN and BBC.

Gavoka says while he initially expressed concern about the impact on Fiji’s tourism industry, he believes being open about the country’s HIV and drug problems will build trust internationally.

He says despite the emergency declaration and global coverage, hotels and airlines remain full because people trust the Fijian Government to address the threats.

Gavoka says the HIV Act, Maritime Powers Bill and Counter-Narcotics Bill demonstrate that Fiji is taking action to address HIV and drugs.

He says the tourism community wants the Counter-Narcotics Bill passed and is calling for support to have it passed as quickly as possible.

item.title: FICAC ordered to bring investigation officer in Prof. Biman Prasad trial over disputed document
item.description: The Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption has been ordered to bring in the investigation officer responsible for putting together the files in former Deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad's FICAC trial. Magistrate Yogesh Prasad has told FICAC counsel Joseph Work to obtain the investigation officer's statement for a voir dire, which is a "trial within a trial" held during court proc
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption has been ordered to bring in the investigation officer responsible for putting together the files in former Deputy Prime Minister Professor Biman Prasad's FICAC trial.

Magistrate Yogesh Prasad has told FICAC counsel Joseph Work to obtain the investigation officer's statement for a voir dire, which is a "trial within a trial" held during court proceedings to determine whether specific evidence is legally admissible.

This relates to a document FICAC tendered last week to be admitted as evidence, the authenticity of which is being disputed by the defence.

Defence counsel Richard Naidu says that for the past eight months or so, the defence had been led to believe by FICAC that the document in its possession was the original.

Naidu says they discovered yesterday that it was a colour copy, and when FICAC produced the original today, it differed from the copy produced earlier as it did not have the Fijian Elections Office stamp.

The court has directed Naidu to send his questions to FICAC by 2pm, while FICAC has been directed to provide him with the investigation officer's statement by 4pm.

Professor Prasad is charged with two offences relating to alleged non-disclosure in his 2015 statutory declaration while he was an office holder of the National Federation Party.

item.title: Racagi death investigation findings with ODPP- Tudravu
item.description: Pita Toganivalu , Vijay Narayan · 29/09/2026 Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu says the investigation into the death of Lami Police Constable Peniasi Racagi is with the Office of the DPP, with police awaiting legal advice before taking further action.
item.content:encoded:
Pita Toganivalu , Vijay Narayan · 29/09/2026

Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu says the investigation into the death of Lami Police Constable Peniasi Racagi is with the Office of the DPP, with police awaiting legal advice before taking further action.

Tudravu was responding to questions on the case during the Police Remembrance Day today.

He says the Police Force understands the concerns of Racagi’s family and the general public about the progress of the investigation.

However, Tudravu says police are guided by established processes and systems.

He says questions about the early arrest made in the case are also part of the investigation process.

Constable Peniasi Racagi was murdered in Lami on the 22nd of February this year.

Police had earlier stated that their investigations focused into two avenues of the officer's death and Police involvement.
